items.text: 6 CHEMICAL FORMULAE, EQUATIONS AND CALCULATIONS: PART 2

items.label: text
items.text: In this chapter we will look at how to extend our understanding of moles to carry out calculations involving gases and solutions. You need to have studied the material covered in Chapter 5 before starting on this chapter.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 6.2 Three identical flasks containing different gases at the same temperature and pressure all contain equal numbers of molecules.

items.label: text
items.text: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

items.label: text
items.text: This means that if you have 100 cm³ of hydrogen at some temperature and pressure, it contains exactly the same number of molecules as there are in 100 cm³ of Cl2, or any other gas under those conditions, irrespective of the size of the molecules.

items.label: text
items.text: You can see how this works in a chemical reaction. Methane (CH4) reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water. The equation for the reaction is:

items.label: formula
items.text: C H _ { 4 } ( g ) + 2 O _ { 2 } ( g ) \rightarrow C O _ { 2 } ( g ) + 2 H _ { 2 } O ( I )

items.label: text
items.text: We need two O2 molecules to react with each CH4 molecule, so if we react 100 cm³ of CH4 we will need twice the volume of O2 to obtain the correct number of particles. In this equation, 100 cm³ of methane will react exactly with 200 cm³ of oxygen gas and 100 cm³ of carbon dioxide gas will be formed.

items.label: text
items.text: For helium and the other noble gases we would use the word 'atoms' instead of 'molecules'.
